prompt: In `qkv.py` the hard lookup returned 20 and the soft lookup 24.04. Why is the soft result higher?
hint: Look at the weights the softmax gave the four keys.

choices.text: The softmax rounded the weights up
choices.why: The weights printed sum to 1.0; nothing was rounded in either direction.

choices.text: Every value contributed, weighted by how well its key matched
choices.why: Right. Weights of 0.232 on 30 and 0.172 on 40 pull harder than 0.172 on 10, so the result lands above 20.

choices.text: The query matched the third key best
choices.why: It scored 0.9 against the second key and 0.3 against the third; the second won.

choices.text: The soft lookup adds a bias of its own to every result it returns
choices.why: There is no bias in it: the result is the weights times the values, and nothing else.

prompt: Why does attention mix all the values with a softmax instead of returning the value of the best-matching key?
hint: Think about what training needs from every step of the computation.

choices.text: Picking the best key is slower than a softmax on a processor
choices.why: `argmax` is cheap. Speed is not what rules it out.

choices.text: A softmax makes the output a probability distribution over the four keys
choices.why: The weights sum to 1, but the output is a mixture of value vectors, not a distribution.

choices.text: Choosing one key has no gradient, so where to look cannot be learnt
choices.why: Right. The soft lookup gave a gradient for the query; `argmax` changes nothing until the winner jumps.

choices.text: Several keys could tie for the best match, and a tie has no winner to return
choices.why: Ties are rare with real numbers, and a rule to break them would be easy. The gradient is the reason.

prompt: A query and a key each have 256 random features with a spread of 1. About what spread do their dot products have, before any scaling?
In `attention.py`, row 2 of the weights is nearly flat: 0.258, 0.265, 0.171, 0.307. What does that say about the second token's output?
hint: Each output row is the weights of its row times the values.

choices.text: It is zero, because no key matched
choices.why: Weights that sum to 1 never give zero by themselves: the output is a mix of the values.

choices.text: It is close to the plain average of the four values
choices.why: Right. With nearly equal weights, the mix is nearly an average.

choices.text: Mostly the fourth value, as 0.307 is largest
choices.why: 0.307 is less than a third. Compare row 1, where 0.741 on one key does make the output mostly that value.

choices.text: It equals the second token's own value
choices.why: Its weight on itself is 0.265; a token only returns its own value when that weight is 1.

prompt: A colleague removes the division by √d from a model whose heads are 1,024 wide. What happens at the start of training?
hint: Work out the spread of the scores at that width, then think about the softmax.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since Adam rescales every parameter's gradient to a similar size anyway
choices.why: Adam rescales per parameter, but it cannot restore a slope the softmax has already flattened towards zero.

choices.text: The scores shrink and every weight becomes nearly equal
choices.why: The opposite: without the division the scores grow, with a spread of about 32 here.

choices.text: Each softmax puts nearly all its weight on one key, and passes back little gradient
choices.why: Right. At width 512 the largest weight already took 0.948; at 1,024 the scores spread wider still.

choices.text: The model trains better, because its attention is already sharp at the very first step
choices.why: Sharp before training means sharp at random, on keys nothing has chosen yet.

prompt: Why are the masked scores set to minus infinity rather than to 0?
hint: What does the softmax do with a score of 0?

choices.text: exp(−∞) is 0, so those weights vanish; a score of 0 still gets weight
choices.why: Right. The exponential of 0 is 1, so a zeroed score would still take a share of the row.

choices.text: A score of 0 would make the row add up to more than 1 after the softmax
choices.why: The softmax always divides by the row's total, so every row sums to 1 whatever the scores.

choices.text: Minus infinity makes the gradient larger for the earlier tokens
choices.why: The masked weights are exactly 0 and pass back nothing; the earlier tokens' gradients come from their own weights.

choices.text: 0 is reserved for padding tokens in PyTorch
choices.why: PyTorch reserves no score value for anything; padding is masked the same way, with minus infinity.

prompt: A model reads a whole product review and then says whether it is positive. Should its attention use a causal mask?
hint: The mask exists for one situation. Is this it?

choices.text: Yes, or each token copies the label from the next one
choices.why: There is one label for the whole review, not one per token, so there is nothing ahead to copy.

choices.text: Yes, since every transformer block needs the mask
choices.why: BERT and this lesson's recall model use none. The mask belongs to a task, not to the block.

choices.text: No: the whole text is there before the answer
choices.why: Right. The mask is for predicting what has not been seen yet, which is not this task.

choices.text: No, because a mask only works with a single head
choices.why: A mask applies to every head alike; the reason to skip it here is the task.

prompt: How many parameters does `nn.MultiheadAttention(64, 8)` have, biases included?
hint: Four matrices of d by d and four bias vectors of d. The number of heads does not enter.

prompt: A layer 16 wide goes from 1 head to 4. What changes?

choices.text: It has four times as many parameters, one set for each head
choices.why: Both counted 1,088. The projections are the same size, only cut differently.

choices.text: Each head attends with 4 of the 16 features and its own softmax
choices.why: Right: four independent sets of weights from the same projections, for the same parameters.

choices.text: Each head sees a different quarter of the tokens, and only those
choices.why: Every head sees every token; what is divided is the features.

choices.text: The scores are divided by √16 instead of √4
choices.why: The other way round: with 4 heads each head is 4 wide and divides by √4.

prompt: Attention with no positions added receives five tokens, then the same five in another order. How do the two outputs compare?

choices.text: They are unrelated, since every score changes
choices.why: Every pair of tokens meets with the same score as before, wherever the two sit.

choices.text: They are identical, row for row, in the original order
choices.why: Each token keeps its own output, so the rows move with the tokens.

choices.text: The same rows, shuffled the same way as the input
choices.why: Right, and `allclose` printed `True`. To attention, a sequence without positions is a set.

choices.text: The same rows, in reverse order
choices.why: They follow the shuffle exactly, whatever it was; reversing is just one shuffle among many.

prompt: A model with a learnt table of 50 positions is given a sequence of 60 tokens. What happens?
hint: Where would the vector for position 55 come from?

choices.text: It extrapolates from the pattern of the last rows
choices.why: A learnt table is a list of rows with no formula behind it, so there is nothing to extrapolate.

choices.text: The lookup fails with `IndexError`: there is no row for those positions
choices.why: Right, as `positions.py` showed. A sinusoidal encoding would compute them, though the model has still never seen them.

choices.text: PyTorch reads the first 50 tokens and drops the rest without a word
choices.why: `nn.Embedding` checks its indices and raised an error; nothing was dropped.

choices.text: Positions 51 to 60 reuse rows 1 to 10
choices.why: Nothing wraps around; asking for row 55 of a table of 50 is an error.

prompt: With the sinusoidal encoding, the dot product of two positions depends only on their ___.
hint: Positions 0 and 3, 10 and 13, and 27 and 30 all gave 5.543.

prompt: In the block of `block.py`, 32 wide with an MLP of 128, which part holds most of the parameters?
hint: Two matrices of 32 by 128 against four of 32 by 32.

choices.text: Attention, with its four projections
choices.why: 4,224 of 12,704: about a third.

choices.text: The MLP
choices.why: Right: 8,352 of 12,704, two thirds, at any width with an MLP four times wider.

choices.text: The two layer norms, which have weights for every token
choices.why: They have a gamma and a beta per feature, not per token: 128 in all.

choices.text: They hold about the same, since attention and MLP are both 32 wide
choices.why: The MLP is 128 wide inside, and that is where its weights are.

prompt: With lesson 14's budget, the transformer reached 1.000 at length 50 and the LSTM 0.144. What explains the difference?
hint: What did `where.py` find the last position doing?

choices.text: The transformer had more parameters
choices.why: It had 10,728 against the LSTM model's 21,640, half as many.

choices.text: The transformer was trained for more steps
choices.why: Same 3,000 steps, same batches, same seeds; only the extra measurement at 250 was new.

choices.text: Position 1 is one step from the last, at any length
choices.why: Right. Its heads put up to 0.999 on position 1; the LSTM had to carry it through 49 rewrites.

choices.text: Its causal mask kept it from being distracted by later symbols
choices.why: It had no mask: only the last position is read, and nothing comes after it.

prompt: Without positions the same model reached 0.171 at length 50. Why is that above the 0.125 of guessing?
hint: What can a model learn from a set of symbols with no order?

choices.text: Some position information still leaks through the embedding
choices.why: The symbol embedding is the same at every position; shuffling showed attention adds none.

choices.text: It is noise, within the spread of guessing
choices.why: All four measurements sat above 0.125, from 0.162 to 0.182: a steady gap, not a wobble.

choices.text: The answer is among the symbols present, and it sees which occur
choices.why: Right. A set of symbols narrows the guess a little; without order it cannot say which came first.

choices.text: Some test sequences also appeared in training
choices.why: The test set comes from its own generator; and the same model with positions shows memorising is not the issue.

prompt: Which of these are true of the attention built in this lesson? Choose every one that is.
hint: Each was printed by one of the lesson's programs.

choices.text: Each row of attention weights sums to 1
choices.why: Right: the softmax runs along each row.

choices.text: Four heads have as many parameters as one, at the same width
choices.why: Right: 1,088 both, in `heads.py`.

choices.text: Without positions, attention still tells the first token from the last
choices.why: Shuffling the input only shuffled the output; nothing tells first from last.

choices.text: On one thread, the transformer trained faster than lesson 14's LSTM
choices.why: Its three runs took 110 seconds against 75 for lesson 14's six; it was not faster here.

choices.text: Under the causal mask, changing the last token leaves the earlier outputs unchanged
choices.why: Right: they moved by 0.000 and the last by 0.535.

prompt: A text grows from 500 tokens to 2,000. By how much does the number of attention weights in one head grow?
hint: The weights are a table with a row per query and a column per key.

choices.text: Four times, like the text
choices.why: That would be one weight per token. The table has a row and a column per token.

choices.text: Sixteen times
choices.why: Right: 500 by 500 becomes 2,000 by 2,000, four times in each direction.

choices.text: Not at all; the number of weights depends on the width d
choices.why: The projection matrices depend on d. The attention weights depend on the length.

choices.text: Twice, since only half of them survive the causal mask
choices.why: The mask zeroes about half of them, but the table is still computed at its full size, and grows sixteenfold.
